newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary expects additional automotive investment.
newsitem.headline: Hungary expects additional automotive investment.

text.p: An automaker and an auto parts supplier have agreed to invest in areas of Hungary recently designated for investment incentives, a government official told Reuters on Wednesday, though she would not identify the companies.

"At least one automaker and one auto parts supplier have already decided to invest in areas where they can get certain benefits," said Anna Szekacs, a Ministry of Finance commissioner working on domestic enterprise development.
"I cannot identify the companies because they have the right to make the announcement," Szekacs said. "But probably very soon they will say something publicly."

She said the companies qualify for exemption from the 18 percent corporate profit tax because they will invest over three billion forints and create at least 300 jobs in an area of low economic development and high unemployement.
The government introduced this concession about a month ago to attact investors to these regions, which are concentrated in northeast and parts of south-west Hungary, Szekacs said.
Parliament has yet to approve the concession, but the government will guarantee the tax exemption to any company that agrees to invest on the condition that it receives it, she said.
Hungary, which built no cars under communism, became an early magnet for foreign automotive investment once the East bloc collapsed.
Adam Opel AG, the German division of U.S. automaker General Motors Corp, and Suzuki Motor Corp each started producing cars in Hungary in 1992.

Now observers speculate that Japanese automaker Toyota Motor Corp may want to build cars in Hungary. And local media have reported that Audi AG, the up-market division of German automaker Volkswagen AG, has been looking at sites for a second car assembly plant in Hungary.

Audi already plans by mid-1998 to start assembling its new TT roadster beside the engine plant it opened in 1994 in Gyor in western Hungary. It has declined to comment on reports it is examining sites for a car plant elsewhere in Hungary.

Toyota, which builds cars in Britain, has said it is considering expanding its European production capacity, and industry observers have speculated that France and Slovakia are potential sites for a new factory.

The company says it has made no decisions. "Our future production plans for Europe are under study, and we expect to come to a decision around the end of this year," said Kevin Perlmutter, corporate communications manager at Toyota Motor Europe Marketing and Engineeering SA.
"Clearly it would make sense if we were to build extra production capacity in Europe for a model in a high-volume segment," he told Reuters from his office in London.
"For example the small-car segment would be a possibility, but we've made absolutely no decisions whatsoever, and we have not said anything about any locations."
But analysts said Hungary could be a logical choice, especially because Hungary will start talks next year on joining the European Union, while Slovakia was recently passed over for consideration.

"Toyota is looking to spread out, and they might be viewing east European markets seriously now because of the growth potential there," David Leggett, an analyst at auto consultancy CSM Europe Ltd, told Reuters.
"The Japanese tend to listen to each other and to set up together," Leggett added. "The fact that Hungary already has a Japanese investor with Suzuki could be a plus factor."
